lessons.title: Distance, midpoints and gradients
lessons.summary: Move between coordinates, lengths, midpoints and gradients without reversing one difference.
lessons.objective: Move between coordinates, lengths, midpoints and gradients without reversing one difference.
lessons.before: Draw the right triangle under the segment. The horizontal and vertical displacements give its two shorter sides.
lessons.ideas:
Distance is \(\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\). A negative displacement still contributes a positive square.

For a segment with midpoint \(M\), its missing end is found by doubling each coordinate of \(M\) and subtracting the corresponding known coordinate.

Gradient is \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\). It is undefined when the horizontal change is zero.
lessons.method:
Leave a surd in exact form unless the question asks for a rounded distance.

Substitute the recovered end into the original coordinate averages.

A negative gradient cannot be a negative length.
mistakes: Add the squared changes before taking a square root.
Averaging x with y mixes the directions.
A negative gradient can come from a positive horizontal change and a negative vertical change.

examples.title: Distance along a survey baseline
examples.question:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(7,0)\) and \(Q(11,20)\).

  1. Find the exact length of the baseline.

    [2]

  2. Find the gradient of the baseline.

    [2]

  3. Find the midpoint of the baseline.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The changes from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(4\) horizontally and \(20\) vertically.

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=416\).

\(4\sqrt{26}\)

(b) Use vertical change over horizontal change: \(\frac{20}{4}\).

\(5\)

(c) Average matched coordinates: \(M=(9,10)\).

\((9,10)\)

examples.title: Recover the other end of a segment
examples.question:
A segment has endpoint \(P(2,3)\) and midpoint \(M(4,-10)\).

  1. Find the other endpoint.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of the baseline.

    [2]

  3. Find the gradient of the baseline.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Double the midpoint coordinate and subtract the known endpoint: \(Q=(4,-10)\times2-(2,3)\).

\((6,-23)\)

(b) The changes from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(4\) horizontally and \(-26\) vertically.

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=692\).

\(2\sqrt{173}\)

(c) Use vertical change over horizontal change: \(\frac{-26}{4}\).

\(-\frac{13}{2}\)

examples.title: The direction of a ramp
examples.question:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-3,6)\) and \(Q(1,38)\).

  1. Find the gradient of the baseline.

    [2]

  2. Find the midpoint of the baseline.

    [2]

  3. A second ramp begins at \(Q\). It has the same gradient. At \(x=3\), find its height coordinate.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use vertical change over horizontal change: \(\frac{32}{4}\).

\(8\)

(b) Average matched coordinates: \(M=(-1,22)\).

\((-1,22)\)

(c) The second ramp moves horizontally by \(2\). Its vertical change is \(16\).

\(54\)

lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
lessons.summary: Use direction conditions to find lines and missing coordinates.
lessons.objective: Use direction conditions to find lines and missing coordinates.
lessons.before: Horizontal progress of one unit produces the same vertical change on parallel lines.
lessons.ideas:
Parallel non-vertical lines have equal gradients. Distinct intercepts give distinct parallel lines.

Non-vertical perpendicular lines have gradient product \(-1\). A horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.

A point lies on a perpendicular bisector precisely when it is the same distance from the two ends.
lessons.method:
Rearrange the given equation for y before reading the gradient.

Test a horizontal or vertical line separately before using a reciprocal.

Find the midpoint and gradient in separate lines of working.
mistakes: A common gradient and intercept describe the same line.
Negating without taking the reciprocal normally produces the wrong angle.
The perpendicular through an endpoint is a different line.

examples.title: Two parallel route lines
examples.question:
The line \(L\) has equation \(3x+11y=0\). A line \(K\) passes through \(P(11,12)\) and is parallel to \(L\).

  1. Find the gradient of \(K\).

    [2]

  2. Find an equation for \(K\).

    [2]

  3. Find the y-coordinate of \(K\) when \(x=22\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Rearrange the given equation to obtain \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x\). Parallel lines have equal gradients.

\(-\frac{3}{11}\)

(b) Substitute \((11,12)\) into \(y=mx+c\) using \(m=-\frac{3}{11}\). The intercept is \(15\).

\(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+15\)

(c) Substitute the new horizontal coordinate into \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+15\).

\(9\)

examples.title: A perpendicular through an off-line point
examples.question:
A segment joins \(A(-1,-12)\) to \(B(3,18)\). The line \(K\) is perpendicular to \(AB\) and passes through \(P(21,-7)\).

  1. Find an equation of \(K\).

    [3]

  2. Find where \(K\) meets the y-axis.

    [2]

  3. State the product of the gradients of \(K\) and \(AB\).

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(AB\) has gradient \(\frac{15}{2}\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{2}{15}\).

Substitute \((21,-7)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=-\frac{21}{5}\).

\(y=-\frac{2}{15}x-\frac{21}{5}\)

(b) Set \(x=0\) in \(y=-\frac{2}{15}x-\frac{21}{5}\).

\((0,-\frac{21}{5})\)

(c) Multiply \(-\frac{2}{15}\) by \(\frac{15}{2}\).

\(-1\)

examples.title: Perpendicular bisector of a baseline
examples.question:
A segment joins \(A(-6,-15)\) to \(B(-2,21)\). Its midfield boundary is the perpendicular bisector.

  1. Find an equation of the perpendicular bisector.

    [3]

  2. Find its intersection with the x-axis.

    [2]

  3. Explain why its midpoint is equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\).

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(AB\) has gradient \(9\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{1}{9}\).

The midpoint is \((-4,3)\). Substitute \((-4,3)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=\frac{23}{9}\).

\(y=-\frac{1}{9}x+\frac{23}{9}\)

(b) Set \(y=0\) in \(y=-\frac{1}{9}x+\frac{23}{9}\) and solve for \(x\).

\((23,0)\)

(c) It lies on the segment and is the same fraction of the original distance from both ends.

A midpoint divides a segment into two equal lengths.

lessons.title: Line equations and intersections
lessons.summary: Write line equations in standard forms and solve for their single shared point.
lessons.objective: Write line equations in standard forms and solve for their single shared point.
lessons.before: A gradient fixes the direction. Substituting one point fixes the remaining constant.
lessons.ideas:
Either use \(y=mx+c\) and solve for \(c\), or write \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\).

If both equations give \(y\), set their right-hand sides equal, then substitute the resulting x-coordinate back.

Forms such as \(ax+by=c\) and \(y=mx+c\) describe the same line when one is obtained by valid rearrangement.
lessons.method:
Check the final equation with both given points when possible.

Use the simpler equation to find y, then verify the pair in the other equation.

Use exact fractions or clear denominators across the whole equation.
mistakes: The y-coordinate of the given point is its intercept only if its x-coordinate is zero.
The x-coordinate alone does not describe the intersection.
The sign of the x-coefficient changes when you move the x-term to the other side.

examples.title: Meet at a point
examples.question:
A path passes through \(A(-8,17)\) and \(B(-4,25)\). A second path lies on \(11x+y=-45\).

  1. Find the equation of the first line.

    [2]

  2. Find the point where the lines cross.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact distance from \((-8,17)\) to the intersection.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use gradient \(2\) and substitute \((-8,17)\) for a point on the line.

\(y=2x+33\)

(b) The second line is \(y=-11x-45\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.

Rearranging gives \(13x=-78\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=21\).

\((-6,21)\)

(c) The coordinate differences are \(2\) and \(4\). Apply Pythagoras.

\(2\sqrt{5}\)

examples.title: When the two readings agree
examples.question:
A motion sensor gives the position \(y=2x+49\). A second sensor gives \(14x+y=-127\).

  1. Find the point where the lines cross.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact distance from \((-13,23)\) to the intersection.

    [2]

  3. Which model has the larger y-value one unit to the right of the intersection? Give the difference.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The second line is \(y=-14x-127\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.

Rearranging gives \(16x=-176\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=27\).

\((-11,27)\)

(b) The coordinate differences are \(2\) and \(4\). Apply Pythagoras.

\(2\sqrt{5}\)

(c) One unit to the right, the first output changes by \(2\) and the second by \(-14\).

The first model, by \(16\).

examples.title: Meet at a point
examples.question:
A straight graph has gradient \(2\) and passes through \(A(1,27)\). It intersects the line \(16x+y=79\).

  1. Find the equation of the first line.

    [2]

  2. Find the point where the lines cross.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact distance from \((1,27)\) to the intersection.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use gradient \(2\) and substitute \((1,27)\) for a point on the line.

\(y=2x+25\)

(b) The second line is \(y=-16x+79\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.

Rearranging gives \(18x=54\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=31\).

\((3,31)\)

(c) The coordinate differences are \(2\) and \(4\). Apply Pythagoras.

\(2\sqrt{5}\)

lessons.title: Areas from coordinates and lines
lessons.summary: Use intercepts or an appropriate diagonal to identify perpendicular heights.
lessons.objective: Use intercepts or an appropriate diagonal to identify perpendicular heights.
lessons.before: The axes meet at right angles. Find their intersections with the third side to identify the base and height.
lessons.ideas:
An x-intercept has \(y=0\) and a y-intercept has \(x=0\). Use their positive distances from the origin in the area formula.

For a vertical base on \(x=c\), a point with x-coordinate \(u\) has perpendicular distance \(|u-c|\) from that line.

Each triangle contributes \(\frac{1}{2}bh\). With a common base, compare their areas by comparing their heights.
lessons.method:
A negative intercept can still give a positive length.

Sketch the base and draw a small perpendicular mark beside the height.

State which base and height you used for each contribution.
mistakes: Find the two intercepts by setting a different coordinate to zero each time.
A sloping side does not normally give the perpendicular height.
Check whether the two heights run to opposite sides of the line before adding the regions.

examples.title: An intercept triangle
examples.question:
The line \(25x+3y=75\) and the positive coordinate axes enclose a triangle.

  1. Give the point where the line meets the x-axis.

    [2]

  2. Find the area of the triangle.

    [2]

  3. The x-intercept doubles and the y-intercept stays fixed. Find the new area.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Set \(y=0\) and divide by \(25\).

\((3,0)\)

(b) Setting \(x=0\) gives a height of \(25\).

The area is \(\frac{1}{2}\times3\times25=\frac{75}{2}\).

\(\frac{75}{2}\) square units.

(c) Doubling the base while keeping the height fixed doubles the area.

\(75\) square units.

examples.title: Triangle with a vertical side
examples.question:
A site plan forms a triangle with vertices \(A(3,10)\), \(B(3,12)\) and \(C(18,9)\).

  1. Find the perpendicular distance from \(C\) to the line \(AB\).

    [2]

  2. Find the area of the triangle.

    [2]

  3. Reflect C in the line AB. Give the reflected point.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The line \(AB\) is vertical, so its perpendicular distance is the horizontal difference.

\(15\)

(b) The base \(AB\) has length \(2\), and the perpendicular height is \(15\).

\(15\) square units.

(c) The y-coordinate is fixed and the reflected x-coordinate is \(-12\).

\((-12,9)\)

examples.title: Split an outline into two triangles
examples.question:
A quadrilateral has vertices \(A(-2,13)\), \(C(16,12)\), \(B(-2,15)\) and \(D(-21,17)\) in that order.

  1. Find the area of the quadrilateral.

    [3]

  2. Find the ratio of the areas of triangles \(ACB\) and \(ADB\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Draw diagonal \(AB\). The horizontal heights on its two sides are \(18\) and \(19\).

The total is \(\frac{1}{2}\times2\times37=37\).

\(37\) square units.

(b) Their bases coincide, so their areas are in the same ratio as their heights.

\(18:19\)

lessons.title: Changing the variables to obtain a straight line
lessons.summary: Choose transformed axes and interpret the gradient and intercept.
lessons.objective: Choose transformed axes and interpret the gradient and intercept.
lessons.before: Undo the outer function first. Then look for one expression of x with a constant multiple and a constant term.
lessons.ideas:
In \(\sqrt y=a+b/x\), the two axis variables can be \(Y=\sqrt y\) and \(X=1/x\). The relation then has the form \(Y=bX+a\).

For \(y=Ax^n\), plot \(\log y\) against \(\log x\). The gradient is \(n\) and the intercept is \(\log A\).

If \(y=e^{ax^2+b}\), use \(Y=\ln y\) and \(X=x^2\). In \(Y=aX+b\), identify the constants by their roles.
lessons.method:
Write the two axis definitions before giving the gradient or intercept.

Use the same base for the logarithms on both axes.

Restore the original x and y after reading the parameters.
mistakes: The heading ‘Y against X’ puts Y on the vertical axis.
The intercept is a logarithm of A. Undo it to find A itself.
Choose a horizontal variable that accounts for the power of x in the exponent.

examples.title: A reciprocal calibration
examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=\left(16+\frac{13}{x}\right)^3\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) on the horizontal axis.

  1. Which expression should go on the vertical axis?

    [2]

  2. Give the gradient and vertical intercept of the transformed line.

    [2]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=13\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Take the positive cube root, then use \(X=\frac{1}{x}\).

That gives \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\) and \(Y=13X+16\).

\(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\)

(b) Write the transformed relation as \(Y=13X+16\).

\(13\) and \(16\), respectively.

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=\left(16+\frac{13}{x}\right)^3\) and simplify.

\(4913\)

examples.title: Recover the exponent of a power
examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=2^{11}x^{16}\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=\log_2 x\) on the horizontal axis.

  1. Which expression should go on the vertical axis?

    [2]

  2. Give the gradient and vertical intercept of the transformed line.

    [2]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=8\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use the product and power laws to convert \(\log_2(Ax^n)\) to \(\log_2 A+n\log_2 x\).

That gives \(Y=\log_2 y\) and \(Y=16X+11\).

\(Y=\log_2 y\)

(b) Write the transformed relation as \(Y=16X+11\).

\(16\) and \(11\), respectively.

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=2^{11}x^{16}\) and simplify.

\(2^{59}\)

examples.title: An exponential calibration
examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=e^{2x^2+5}\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=x^2\) on the horizontal axis.

  1. Which expression should go on the vertical axis?

    [2]

  2. Give the gradient and vertical intercept of the transformed line.

    [2]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=4\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Taking natural logs removes the exponential. Put \(X=x^2\) for its quadratic input.

That gives \(Y=\ln y\) and \(Y=2X+5\).

\(Y=\ln y\)

(b) Write the transformed relation as \(Y=2X+5\).

\(2\) and \(5\), respectively.

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=e^{2x^2+5}\) and simplify.

\(e^{37}\)

lessons.title: Recovering relations from transformed graphs
lessons.summary: Replace transformed variables and undo the corresponding operations in the right order.
lessons.objective: Replace transformed variables and undo the corresponding operations in the right order.
lessons.before: Read the transformed axes literally. A plot of y² against x³ does not give y directly.
lessons.ideas:
If \(Y=y^2\) and \(X=x^3\), use \(y^2=ax^3+b\). Choose the square-root branch using the domain.

From \(e^{2y}=ax^2+b\), take natural logs to get \(2y=\ln(ax^2+b)\) before dividing by two.

If \(X=\ln x\) and \(Y=y^3\), then \(y=\sqrt[3]{a\ln x+b}\).
lessons.method:
If the question gives y positive, explain the branch you use.

The argument of any logarithm must be positive.

Use the model only on the original domain supplied in the question.
mistakes: The root must cover the entire original expression for y².
A factor in the exponent is still present after taking logs.
A cube root of a sum cannot be split into two cube roots.

examples.title: Read back from transformed axes
examples.question:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=y^2\) against \(X=x^3\) has equation \(Y=10X+14\).

  1. Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=2\).

    [2]

  3. Give the transformed vertical intercept and say whether \(x=0\) is allowed.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(y^2=10x^3+14\).

Take the positive square root because \(y>0\).

\(y=\sqrt{10x^3+14}\)

(b) Evaluate the relation \(y=\sqrt{10x^3+14}\) at the original input.

\(\sqrt{94}\)

(c) The graph's vertical intercept uses \(X=0\). A graph intercept can lie outside the given domain, so read it as the parameter of the line.

The intercept is \(14\). The domain requires \(x>0\).

examples.title: Read back from transformed axes
examples.question:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=e^{2y}\) against \(X=x^2\) has equation \(Y=5X+17\).

  1. Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=2\).

    [2]

  3. Give the transformed vertical intercept and say whether \(x=0\) is allowed.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(e^{2y}=5x^2+17\).

Take natural logs and then divide the resulting equation for \(2y\) by two.

\(y=\frac{1}{2}\ln(5x^2+17)\)

(b) Evaluate the relation \(y=\frac{1}{2}\ln(5x^2+17)\) at the original input.

\(\frac{1}{2}\ln 37\)

(c) The graph's vertical intercept uses \(X=0\). A graph intercept can lie outside the given domain, so read it as the parameter of the line.

The intercept is \(17\). The domain requires \(x>0\).

examples.title: Read back from transformed axes
examples.question:
For \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), the graph of \(Y=y^3\) against \(X=\ln x\) has equation \(Y=19X+2\).

  1. Select the resulting equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=e\).

    [2]

  3. Give the transformed vertical intercept and say whether \(x=0\) is allowed.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Replace the axis names by their definitions to get \(y^3=19\ln x+2\).

Take the cube root of the entire right side.

\(y=\sqrt[3]{19\ln x+2}\)

(b) Evaluate the relation \(y=\sqrt[3]{19\ln x+2}\) at the original input.

\(\sqrt[3]{21}\)

(c) The graph's vertical intercept uses \(X=0\). A graph intercept can lie outside the given domain, so read it as the parameter of the line.

The intercept is \(2\). The domain requires \(x>0\).

lessons.title: Finding and using a straight-line model from data
lessons.summary: Read transformed tables, recover original parameters and predict outputs.
lessons.objective: Read transformed tables, recover original parameters and predict outputs.
lessons.before: Use two compatible pairs. Every row must refer to the same choices of X and Y.
lessons.ideas:
Find the gradient in transformed coordinates, substitute one row for the intercept, and test a third row.

For \(y=Ab^x\), a step of \(h\) gives an output ratio of \(b^h\), so recover \(b\) by taking a positive root.

A transformed intercept may give a parameter such as a logarithm of the initial value. Apply the inverse operation to interpret it.
lessons.method:
Label your working columns X and Y before fitting the line.

Use the exact ratio before taking a root.

Check whether the requested value is within the model domain before evaluating.
mistakes: Mixing an original x-value with a transformed Y-value changes the gradient.
A table step of two units gives the square of the one-unit multiplier.
The transformed output is generally not the value requested in the original question.

examples.title: A reciprocal calibration
examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy an unknown relation. The table shows points on the straight line obtained using \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\).
\(X\)\(Y\)
\(1\)\(19\)
\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(\frac{23}{2}\)
\(\frac{1}{3}\)\(9\)

  1. Find the gradient of the straight line.

    [2]

  2. Find an equation relating the original variables.

    [3]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=15\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Compute the change in \(Y\) divided by the change in \(X\) for two rows of the table.

The pairs lie on \(Y=15X+4\).

\(15\)

(b) Use a table point to find the intercept \(4\). The transformed equation is \(\sqrt[3]{y}=4+15X\).

From \(y^{1/3}=4+\frac{15}{x}\) recover the original output by raising both sides to power \(3\).

\(y=\left(4+\frac{15}{x}\right)^3\)

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=\left(4+\frac{15}{x}\right)^3\) and simplify.

\(125\)

examples.title: Find a constant multiplication factor
examples.question:
The measurements in the table are modelled by \(y=Ab_0^x\) with positive constants.
\(x\)\(y\)
\(0\)\(18\)
\(2\)\(162\)
\(4\)\(1458\)

  1. Find the multiplying factor over one unit of x.

    [2]

  2. Find the equation of the untransformed graph.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of the model at \(x=1\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Two steps multiply the output by \(9\). Taking the positive square root gives the multiplier per step.

\(3\)

(b) The zero input is \(18\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(3\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{3}y=x+\log_{3}18\) would use the gradient \(1\).

\(y=18(3)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(3\).

\(54\)

examples.title: An exponential calibration
examples.question:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy an unknown relation. The table shows points on the straight line obtained using \(X=x^2\) and \(Y=\ln y\).
\(X\)\(Y\)
\(1\)\(15\)
\(4\)\(24\)
\(9\)\(39\)

  1. Find the gradient of the straight line.

    [2]

  2. Find an equation relating the original variables.

    [3]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=4\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Compute the change in \(Y\) divided by the change in \(X\) for two rows of the table.

The pairs lie on \(Y=3X+12\).

\(3\)

(b) Use a table point to find the intercept \(12\). The transformed equation is \(\ln y=3X+12\).

Use \(y=e^Y\) to return from the transformed graph to the original output.

\(y=e^{3x^2+12}\)

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=e^{3x^2+12}\) and simplify.

\(e^{60}\)

questions.title: Distance along a survey baseline
questions.prompt_html:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(0,6)\) and \(Q(6,38)\).

Find the exact length of the baseline.
questions.solution_html:
The changes from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(6\) horizontally and \(32\) vertically.

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=1060\).

\(2\sqrt{265}\)
questions.hint_html: Use the squares of coordinate differences.

questions.title: Distance along a survey baseline
questions.prompt_html:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(3,6)\) and \(Q(9,38)\).

Find the exact length of the baseline.
questions.solution_html:
The changes from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(6\) horizontally and \(32\) vertically.

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=1060\).

\(2\sqrt{265}\)
questions.hint_html: Use the squares of coordinate differences.

questions.title: Recover the other end of a segment
questions.prompt_html:
A segment has endpoint \(P(-11,7)\) and midpoint \(M(-8,-10)\).

Find the other endpoint.
questions.solution_html:
Double the midpoint coordinate and subtract the known endpoint: \(Q=(-8,-10)\times2-(-11,7)\).

\((-5,-27)\)
questions.hint_html: Use each midpoint equation in reverse.

questions.title: Recover the other end of a segment
questions.prompt_html:
A segment has endpoint \(P(-8,7)\) and midpoint \(M(-5,-10)\).

Find the other endpoint.
questions.solution_html:
Double the midpoint coordinate and subtract the known endpoint: \(Q=(-5,-10)\times2-(-8,7)\).

\((-2,-27)\)
questions.hint_html: Use each midpoint equation in reverse.

questions.title: The direction of a ramp
questions.prompt_html:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-3,7)\) and \(Q(3,41)\).

Find the gradient of the baseline.

questions.title: When the two readings agree

A motion sensor gives the position \(y=4x+7\). A second sensor gives \(5x+y=7\).

Find the point where the lines cross.

questions.title: A reciprocal calibration
questions.prompt_html:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=\left(9+\frac{10}{x}\right)^3\). A straight graph is drawn with \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) on the horizontal axis.

Which expression should go on the vertical axis?
questions.solution_html:
Take the positive cube root, then use \(X=\frac{1}{x}\).

That gives \(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\) and \(Y=10X+9\).

\(Y=\sqrt[3]{y}\)
questions.hint_html: Undo the outside operation to get a linear expression in X.

A positive quantity has the form \(y=Ab_0^x\). Two exact readings are \(y=5\) at \(x=0\) and \(y=20480\) at \(x=3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:

(b) The zero input is \(5\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(16\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{4}y=2x+\log_{4}5\) would use the gradient \(2\).

\(y=5(16)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(16\).

questions.title: Find a constant multiplication factor
questions.prompt_html:
A positive quantity has the form \(y=Ab_0^x\). Two exact readings are \(y=21\) at \(x=0\) and \(y=86016\) at \(x=3\).

  1. Find the value of \(b_0\).

    [2]

  2. Find the equation of the untransformed graph.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of the model at \(x=1\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The zero input gives \(A=21\). Divide the second value by \(21\) and take the positive cube root.

\(16\)

(b) The zero input is \(21\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(16\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{4}y=2x+\log_{4}21\) would use the gradient \(2\).

\(y=21(16)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(16\).

\(336\)

questions.title: Find a constant multiplication factor
questions.prompt_html:
A positive quantity has the form \(y=Ab_0^x\). Two exact readings are \(y=18\) at \(x=0\) and \(y=281250\) at \(x=3\).

    [2]

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of the model at \(x=1\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The zero input gives \(A=18\). Divide the second value by \(18\) and take the positive cube root.

\(25\)

(b) The zero input is \(18\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(25\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{5}y=2x+\log_{5}18\) would use the gradient \(2\).

\(y=18(25)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(25\).

\(450\)

A positive quantity has the form \(y=Ab_0^x\). Two exact readings are \(y=18\) at \(x=0\) and \(y=3888\) at \(x=3\).

  1. Find the value of \(b_0\).

    [2]

  2. Find the equation of the untransformed graph.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of the model at \(x=1\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The zero input gives \(A=18\). Divide the second value by \(18\) and take the positive cube root.

\(6\)

(b) The zero input is \(18\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(6\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{6}y=x+\log_{6}18\) would use the gradient \(1\).

\(y=18(6)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(6\).

\(108\)
questions.hint_html: Use the ratio of outputs three steps apart.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the ratio of outputs three steps apart.
Use the initial value and per-step multiplier.

questions.title: A reciprocal calibration
questions.prompt_html:
The positive variables \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy an unknown relation. The table shows points on the straight line obtained using \(X=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(Y=\sqrt{y}\).
\(X\)\(Y\)
\(1\)\(27\)
\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(18\)
\(\frac{1}{3}\)\(15\)

  1. Find the gradient of the straight line.

    [2]

  2. Find an equation relating the original variables.

    [3]

  3. Use the relation to find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=18\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Compute the change in \(Y\) divided by the change in \(X\) for two rows of the table.

The pairs lie on \(Y=18X+9\).

\(18\)

(b) Use a table point to find the intercept \(9\). The transformed equation is \(\sqrt{y}=9+18X\).

From \(y^{1/2}=9+\frac{18}{x}\) recover the original output by raising both sides to power \(2\).

\(y=\left(9+\frac{18}{x}\right)^2\)

(c) Substitute the original \(x\) coordinate into \(y=\left(9+\frac{18}{x}\right)^2\) and simplify.

\(100\)
questions.hint_html: Find the gradient from two transformed pairs.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the gradient from two transformed pairs.

A positive quantity has the form \(y=Ab_0^x\). Two exact readings are \(y=21\) at \(x=0\) and \(y=979776\) at \(x=3\).

  1. Find the value of \(b_0\).

    [2]

  2. Find the equation of the untransformed graph.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of the model at \(x=1\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The zero input gives \(A=21\). Divide the second value by \(21\) and take the positive cube root.

\(36\)

(b) The zero input is \(21\). Each one-unit step in \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(36\).

The transformed equation \(\log_{6}y=2x+\log_{6}21\) would use the gradient \(2\).

\(y=21(36)^x\)

(c) Multiply the initial value by one power of \(36\).

\(756\)
questions.hint_html: Use the ratio of outputs three steps apart.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the ratio of outputs three steps apart.
Use the initial value and per-step multiplier.
